# Session 3 - Practical VF: exploring data through graphs


Return to the dataset you used in practical 2. The aim of this session is to carry out an **exploratory analysis**, looking for differences between groups, an interesting association, an unusual value or a lack of pattern worth investigating. There is no particular result you are expected to find, as this will depend on the choices you make.

You may submit this work individually or in pairs, and we strongly encourage you to work together to discuss your choices and mistakes!

There are six stages, and some of the code is already provided in executable cells. Graphs to borrow from the course are identified by their **block number and title**. Copy the block into your own environment, keep its title comment and adapt it to your data. Make sure you run the cells in order to avoid redefining variables incorrectly.

## A. Get your bearings


Save this file alongside the `data` folder from practical 2 and rename it `Session3_VF_SURNAME_Firstname`, keeping its extension. For a pair, include both names. The [five practical datasets](https://flo-unige.github.io/analyse-donnees-statistiques/donnees/) are the same as those used in the previous session. Each file describes 195 countries, with one row per country, for 2021 or 2022.

| Dataset | File inside `data/` |
|---|---|
| Ecological and social transition | `transition_ecologique_sociale_2021.csv` |
| Energy | `energie_2021.csv` |
| Climate impact | `impact_climatique_2021.csv` |
| Water | `eau_2022.csv` |
| Biodiversity | `biodiversite_2022.csv` |


Open the document in RStudio and select **Session > Set Working Directory > To Source File Location** to work in the practical's folder. Use the green triangles to run blocks and write your answers in the spaces provided outside the code. The ggplot2 package is needed for boxes and violins, so if it is not installed, run `install.packages("ggplot2")` once in the console.


The data-loading block is provided below, so you only need to change the CSV path. Keep this as the only loading step, as course Blocks 1, 4 and 8 also read the water dataset and those lines should not be copied again later in the practical.


```{r charger}
library(ggplot2)
donnees <- read.csv("...", fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
head(donnees)
names(donnees)
cat("n =", nrow(donnees), "\n")
length(unique(donnees$country_code))
```

Possible measurements include electricity use per capita, GHG emissions per capita, material footprint per capita, access to drinking water, etc. Find the exact column name in the output from A, then formulate a question about differences between the groups.

## C. Examine the dataset

The following code sets up the categories, putting income groups in their natural order and sorting the other categories to make them easier to read.


```{r ordre}
ordre <- sort(unique(na.omit(donnees[[groupe]])))
if (groupe == "income_group") {
  ordre <- c("low_income", "lower_middle_income",
             "upper_middle_income", "high_income")
}
```

## D. Compare distributions


**Questions:** Before plotting, what difference or similarity between groups seems plausible?



**Your answer:** ...


The code below keeps only rows where both G and Y are available. In this copy of the table, the columns are given the short names `G` and `Y`, referring to your choices in B. The count table helps you compare data availability across groups.


```{r preparer_groupes}
comparaison <- donnees[complete.cases(donnees[c(groupe, colonne_y)]), c(groupe, colonne_y)]
names(comparaison) <- c("G", "Y")
comparaison$G <- factor(comparaison$G, levels = ordre)
total <- table(factor(donnees[[groupe]], levels = ordre))
disponibles <- table(comparaison$G)
print(data.frame(G = ordre, total = as.integer(total),
                 disponibles = as.integer(disponibles),
                 manquantes = as.integer(total - disponibles)))
limites_y <- range(comparaison$Y)
marge <- max(diff(limites_y) * 0.05, 0.01)
limites_y <- limites_y + c(-marge, marge)
```

The `comparaison` table we have just created contains the value of your variable `Y` and your chosen category `G` for each country with usable data, meaning that rows with missing values have been left out.

```{r f1aaa1f5}
comparaison
```

If no values are available, return to B and choose another variable. When a group contains only one value, you cannot describe its spread, so mention this in your interpretation. If too few values are available to compare the groups, choose another variable and explain why. Keep the same vertical limits for both figures to make them easier to compare.

As we saw in the course, the violin's width helps us see where values are concentrated, but it does not directly represent the number of countries. Its outline depends on the smoothing used, while the points show values actually present in the file. Several countries may share the same value and appear in the same place, so keep the counts nearby to avoid overlooking them. If a group has few values, look at the points first before interpreting the violin's shape.

## E. Explore relationships


We will now look at whether Y seems related to another numerical variable, which we will call **X1**. Choose a variable different from Y, explain why the relationship interests you, then enter its exact name and unit in the code below.

```{r premiere_piste}
colonne_x1 <- "EXACT_NAME_X1"
etiquette_x1 <- "X1 (unit)"
paires <- donnees[complete.cases(donnees[c(colonne_x1, colonne_y, groupe)]),
                   c(colonne_x1, colonne_y, groupe)]
names(paires) <- c("X1", "Y", "G")
cat("n =", nrow(paires), "; excluded =", nrow(donnees)-nrow(paires), "\n")
```

We also keep G in the table because we will use it later to distinguish the groups in the scatterplot. Check how many countries are still available, and if the selection is empty, very small or a variable always has the same value, reconsider your choice of variables and explain the problem.


```{r 0e224285}
paires
```

### Look at one possibility differently


Choose the relationship you would like to explore further, using X1 or X2, and briefly explain why. The code below draws the scatterplot again, using colour and shape to distinguish groups so you can see whether your first impression also holds within them or whether they occupy different parts of the plot. You only need to adapt `axe` and `etiquette_x`, while keeping the same countries.


```{r groupes_nuage}
axe <- "X1"
etiquette_x <- etiquette_x1
ggplot(paires, aes(x = .data[[axe]], y = Y,
                   colour = factor(G), shape = factor(G))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65) +
  labs(x = etiquette_x, y = etiquette_y,
       colour = etiquette_groupe, shape = etiquette_groupe)
```

### Optional: a count grid

If many points overlap, you can try **Block 9: Count grid** instead of the grouped view.

The grid groups countries into intervals of X and Y, then uses colour to show how many countries fall in each cell. It therefore represents neither a mean nor a correlation. The boundaries used in the course are for the water dataset, so replace them with boundaries suited to your variables using the preparation below.

```{r grille_preparation}
axe <- "X1"
etiquette_x <- etiquette_x1
limites_x <- seq(min(paires[[axe]]), max(paires[[axe]]), length.out = 11)
limites_grille_y <- seq(min(paires$Y), max(paires$Y), length.out = 11)
```

In Block 9, do not copy the lines defining the course graph's boundaries, as you have just prepared your own. Use `aes(x = .data[[axe]], y = Y)` and `breaks = list(x = limites_x, y = limites_grille_y)` to plot your variables using these new intervals.


Remember to adapt the titles and units, and make it clear in the legend that colour represents a number of countries. If a variable always has the same value, keep the scatterplot instead of using this grid.

To see what grouping changes, you can replace 11 with 6 in both lines that prepare the boundaries (in the code block above), moving from ten to five intervals on each axis. Look at what becomes easier to see and what disappears, without choosing a grid just to support your initial idea.


## F. Select a finding and conclude


To finish, choose a figure from D or E that helps you present your main finding, without producing a new one. Give it a title describing what you observe, then check that the axes, units, legend and number of countries are clearly stated.

Write a few lines introducing the dataset and year, your final question and what the figure shows. Explain how your attempts changed your reading, then suggest a question to investigate further and the additional data that could help answer it.

Consider the limitations relevant to your analysis, such as countries with missing values, small groups or differences in indicator definitions. What we observe between countries does not necessarily describe individuals, and the countries available do not automatically form a random sample. It is perfectly acceptable to conclude that no clear relationship appears, as what matters is explaining your reasoning.
